interest: This file is particularly valuable to historians because it preserves contemporaneous U.S. military intelligence assessments of high-ranking Imperial Japanese Army leaders during the pivotal autumn of 1940, immediately following Japan's signing of the Tripartite Pact and its military entry into northern French Indochina. Compiled by U.S. Military Attaché Harry I. T. Creswell, the reports capture American awareness of strategic command appointments: Raishiro Sumita's assignment to cut off Nationalist China's southern supply lines through Indochina, Kenji Doihara's elevation to the Supreme Military Council after years of covert intelligence operations in Manchuria and North China, and Gen Sugiyama's installation as Chief of the Army General Staff. In addition to offering concise, official career chronologies, the file reveals how U.S. intelligence evaluated the personal reputations, diplomatic dispositions, and factional standing of Japanese generals who would direct operations during World War II in the Pacific.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.21/5, cross-indexed under Army Maneuvers) comprises three biographic military intelligence reports (Nos. 10,218, 10,219, and 10,220) prepared on October 15, 1940, by Lieutenant Colonel Harry I. T. Creswell, U.S. Military Attaché in Tokyo, for the War Department General Staff Military Intelligence Division (G-2) and subsequently forwarded to the Department of State. The reports provide detailed chronological career summaries, decorations, and reputational appraisals for three prominent Imperial Japanese Army general officers following recent high-level reassignments: Major General Raishiro Sumita, newly appointed to head the Japanese military inspectorate in French Indochina; Lieutenant General Kenji Doihara, seasoned intelligence operative and China hand appointed to the Supreme Military Council; and General Gen Sugiyama, former War Minister who was elevated to Chief of the Army General Staff. Together, the documents illustrate American intelligence tracking of the leadership cadre steering Japan's military expansion across China and Southeast Asia at a critical turning point preceding the Pacific War.

subfiles.about: A biographical military intelligence report outlining the military career and qualifications of Major General Raishiro Sumita upon his appointment to head the Japanese inspectorate in French Indochina.
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Lieut. Colonel, Acting General Staff, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Colonel Harry I. T. Creswell transmits a detailed career summary of Major General Raishiro Sumita based on Japanese press and official publications. Sumita, an artillery specialist who graduated with highest honors from the Military Academy, Artillery and Engineers School, and Army Staff College, had previously served as military attaché to France and Belgium and commandant of the Army Heavy Artillery School. The report highlights his recent appointment replacing General Nishihara as head of the Japanese inspectorate in French Indochina tasked with halting traffic into China. Creswell observes that Sumita is highly regarded within the Japanese Army and made a favorable impression during his diplomatic service in France.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,218: Major General Raishiro Sumita
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff

subfiles.about: A biographical intelligence report detailing the career, intelligence activities, and command history of Lieutenant General Kenji Doihara following his appointment to the Supreme Military Council.
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Lieut. Colonel, Acting General Staff, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This intelligence report chronicles the career of Lieutenant General Kenji Doihara in connection with his appointment to the Supreme Military Council on September 28, 1940. It highlights Doihara's extensive covert background in China and Manchuria, including intelligence work under General Shigeru Honjo, advisory roles to Marshal Chang Tso-lin and Marshal Chang Hsueh-liang, and leadership of the Kwantung Army's Special Service Office in Mukden during the 1931 Mukden Incident. The report also outlines his combat commands during the Sino-Japanese War, including the 14th Division's operations along the Peking-Hankow railway. Creswell notes that Doihara is widely recognized as one of the Japanese Army's foremost experts on Chinese affairs, and his appointment to the council ensures senior military leadership has direct access to his specialized knowledge.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,219: Lieut. General Kenji Doihara
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff

subfiles.about: A biographical intelligence report detailing the military career, political posts, and strategic leadership of General Gen Sugiyama upon his appointment as Chief of the Army General Staff.
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Creswell, Lieut. Colonel, Acting General Staff, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This report traces the career of General Gen Sugiyama following his elevation to Chief of the Army General Staff. It outlines his path from the Russo-Japanese War through senior leadership roles, including founding work in army aviation, service as Vice-Minister of War, resignation as Vice Chief of Staff to take responsibility for the February 26, 1936 Incident, and his tenure as Minister of War in the first Konoe Cabinet at the outbreak of the war with China. The document also notes his subsequent leadership of the Japanese Expeditionary Forces in North China succeeding General Count Terauchi. Creswell assesses Sugiyama as a respected, strong-willed disciplinarian with pleasant diplomatic manners whose selection as Chief of Staff was universally approved within Japan.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,220: General Gen Sugiyama
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff
